hints: A confidence interval for a mean has the form $\bar{x} \pm z \times \dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$. Careful: 2.6 is the **variance**, so the standard deviation is its square root. Write $7.1 \pm z \times \sqrt{\dfrac{2.6}{75}}$.
A 92% interval is central, so the 8% outside is split equally into two tails. Find $z$ with $\Phi(z) = $ the area to the left of the upper end (inverse normal on your calculator).
Put your $z$ into both the minus and the plus version of the formula, work out the two ends, and quote them to 3 significant figures as an interval "… to …".
walkthrough:
**What a confidence interval is**

We have one sample of 75 people with mean waiting time $\bar{x} = 7.1$ minutes. The true mean waiting time $\mu$ of everyone is unknown. A 92% confidence interval is a range around 7.1 built so that 92% of intervals made this way would contain $\mu$.

The general form is $\bar{x} \pm z \times \dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$, where $\sigma$ is the population standard deviation and $n$ is the sample size.

**Write the formula with our numbers (this earns the M1)**

Careful with the wording: the question gives the **variance** $\sigma^2 = 2.6$ (units minutes$^2$), not the standard deviation. The formula needs $\sigma$, so we use $\sqrt{\sigma^2/n}$ directly:

$$7.1 \pm z \times \sqrt{\dfrac{2.6}{75}}$$

Using 2.6 as if it were the standard deviation (and squaring it) is the slip the mark scheme mentions.

**Find $z$ for 92% (this earns the B1)**

The interval is in the middle of the normal curve. The 92% is in the middle, so 8% is left over, shared equally between the two tails: 4% in each tail.

The area to the left of the upper end is therefore $100\% - 4\% = 96\%$:

$$\Phi(z) = 0.96$$

On your calculator use the inverse normal (InvNorm) with area $0.96$, mean $0$ and standard deviation $1$ → it shows $1.7506\ldots$. To 3 decimal places:

$$z = 1.751$$

**Calculate the standard error**

The standard deviation of the sample mean is $\sqrt{\dfrac{2.6}{75}}$. Divide first:

$$\dfrac{2.6}{75} = 0.034667\ldots$$

Then square root:

$$\sqrt{0.034667} = 0.18619\ldots$$

**Find how far each end is from 7.1**

$$z \times \sqrt{\dfrac{2.6}{75}} = 1.751 \times 0.18619 = 0.32602\ldots$$

This amount is added to give the upper end and subtracted to give the lower end.

**Work out the two ends (this earns the A1)**

Lower end: $7.1 - 0.32602 = 6.77398\ldots$, which is $6.77$ to 3 significant figures.

Upper end: $7.1 + 0.32602 = 7.42602\ldots$, which is $7.43$ to 3 significant figures.

The answer must be written as an interval, not as a single number.

**Final answer**

The 92% confidence interval for the population mean waiting time is $$6.77 \text{ to } 7.43 \text{ minutes (3 s.f.)}$$

hints: A 92% interval misses the true mean 8% of the time. That 8% is split between intervals that lie wholly above $\mu$ and intervals that lie wholly below $\mu$. Decide what share belongs to "wholly above".

The three intervals come from independent samples, so the probability that all three do this is the product of three equal probabilities: raise your single-interval probability to the power 3 and quote the result.
walkthrough:
**Understand when an interval lies wholly above the true mean**

A 92% confidence interval contains the true mean $\mu$ with probability 0.92. So the probability that it does **not** contain $\mu$ is $1 - 0.92 = 0.08$.

When an interval misses $\mu$, there are two ways: it can lie entirely **above** $\mu$ (the sample mean was unusually high), or entirely **below** $\mu$ (unusually low). By the symmetry of the normal distribution these two are equally likely.

**Probability for one interval (this earns the M1 when cubed)**

$$\text{P}(\text{one interval entirely above } \mu) = \dfrac{0.08}{2} = 0.04$$

This is the same 4% tail we used to find $z$ in part (a).

**Three independent intervals**

The three samples are independent, so we multiply the three probabilities. Each is 0.04:

$$0.04^3 = 0.04 \times 0.04 \times 0.04$$

$$0.04 \times 0.04 = 0.0016$$

$$0.0016 \times 0.04 = 0.000064$$

(Using $0.08^3$ instead — forgetting to halve — earns the M1 only, not the A1.)

hints: A sample for a confidence interval must represent all people who wait at the bus stop. Think about what is special about taking the first 75 people on one Monday morning.
walkthrough:
**What a suitable sample must be**

Confidence-interval formulas assume the sample is **random** and representative of the whole population: every person who waits at the bus stop should have had an equal chance of being chosen, at any time and on any day.

**Why this sample fails**

The first 75 people on a Monday morning are all from one particular day and time of day. Waiting times at rush hour on a Monday could be quite different from the waiting times in the afternoon, at weekends or on other days. So the sample is not random and not representative.

**Final answer**

The sample is unsuitable because it is taken at one particular day and time of day (it is not a random sample of all people who wait at the bus stop).
